Although blocking-temperature spectra are somewhat lower and more distributed than in the gabbro, directions are indistinguishable; behaviours contrast with slate in the granite aureole (Section 4b) and record thermal overprinting by the gabbro complex. Three episodes of folding (F1–F3) have been recognized in the Skiddaw Slate Group immediately to the south of the Carrock Fell Complex by Roberts (1971). The Layered Gabbros are in the northern limb of a large regional-scale F2 fold with ENE–WSW trending axis (Figure 7). Tight upright folds of the F1 generation are only

ecognized close to the intrusive contact with the Skiddaw Granite (sites 1 and 2 in Figure 12). Where strong magnetizations are present they are largely unblocked in the ﬁrst stages of treatment, mostly below 2008C, and are likely to reside in secondary multidomain carriers grown during thermal metamorphism. At greater distances from the granite contact components deﬁned by thermal demagnetization reﬂect the overprinting e ects of the granite and are more prominent in this body than in the Layered Gabbros or Granophyre (Figure 14). Other samples have a SSW ChRM following removal of a present ﬁeld component (sample 3-4 in Figure 13). This is magnetite-held like the granite overprints and, since it is also close to the Early Carboniferous palaeoﬁeld direction, cannot positively be identiﬁed as older than the granite. However, overprinting of this age is not recognized elsewhere in the region; furthermore four samples illustrate a reversal in this component (sample 5-5 in Figure 13). The angle between axes deﬁned by the normal and reversed components is 11.08, which is less than the critical angle of 15.28 and yields a positive class C reversal test (McFadden and McElhinny, 1990). Ocean closure and suturing resulted in Late Ordovician and Acadian tectonism and were accompanied by emplacement of a large regional batholith. Palaeomagnetic study of intrusive igneous rocks, including application of thermal demagnet- ization, ﬁeld tests and principal component analysis, identiﬁes a history of Ordovician to Devonian magnetization. Although this axis is recorded as a sporadic overprint in older rocks, no pervasive remagnetization is attributable to batholith emplacement. These identify impersistent WNW–ESE trending anomalies; outcrop was detected and sampled at seven of these anomalies (sites 1-5 and 7 in Figure 11b plus an additional site (6) near Wastwater Lake to the east). Whilst intrusion ages are uncertain, an origin related to emplacement with, or soon after, the granophyre is probable because they are not observed in the younger Eskdale Granite. Site 7 is in basic facies of the granophyre pluton. Site 6 near Wastwater Lake may have a di erent origin because a dyke-like form is suggested by a long linear outcrop with discrete contacts. The exception is site 4 (e.g. sample 4-5 in Figure 11a) where single and very stable NNW positive components are present. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. he ﬁnal phase of subduction-related magmatism at this margin of Avalonia. Following cessation of volcanism, a transgressing sea deposited limestones, shales, mudstones and greywackes between Late Caradoc and Ludlow times. This succession forms the Winderemere Supergroup and makes up the Silurian outcrop in Figure 1. During burial and subsequent Acadian deformation the Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Lake District were metamorphosed to no higher than lower greenschist grade, in common with the paratectonic Caledonides of Wales; this was insucient to comprehensively remagnetize pre-Acadian rocks which are reported widely to retain an Ordovician remanence record (Briden and Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978; Piper, 1979; Channell and McCabe, 1992). In addition to the basic plutonism noted above, acidic magmatism occurred at various stages between the intense mid-Ordovician volcanic events and the culmination of tectonic activity in the Acadian episode. A general distinction is recognized between earlier Na-rich activity and later more K-rich activity (Piper et al., 1978). Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. We report U–Pb ages and palaeomagnetic results for two suites of maﬁc sills within the intracratonic Bangemall Basin of Western Australia, one of which is dated at 1070 ± 6 Ma and carries a high-stability palaeomagnetic remanence. Comparison of the Bangemall palaeopole with Laurentian data suggests that previous reconstructions of eastern Australia against either western Canada (SWEAT) or the western United States (AUSWUS) are not viable at 1070 Ma. This implies that the Paciﬁc Ocean did not form by separation of Australia–Antarc- tica from Laurentia, and that up to 10 000 km of late Neoproterozoic passive margins need to be matched with other continental blocks within any proposed Rodinia supercontinent. We report U–Pb ages and palaeomagnetic results for two suites of maﬁc sills within the intracratonic Bangemall Basin of Western Australia, one of which is dated at 1070 ± 6 Ma and carries a high-stability palaeomagnetic remanence. Comparison of the Bangemall palaeopole with Laurentian data suggests that previous reconstructions of eastern Australia against either western Canada (SWEAT) or the western United States (AUSWUS) are not viable at 1070 Ma. This implies that the Paciﬁc Ocean did not form by separation of Australia–Antarc- tica from Laurentia, and that up to 10 000 km of late Neoproterozoic passive margins need to be matched with other continental blocks within any proposed Rodinia supercontinent. Our results permit a reconstruction (AUSMEX) that closely aligns late Mesoproterozoic orogenic belts in north-east Australia and southernmost Laurentia. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: iversity, Kobe 657-8501, Japan Received 27 May 2001; received in revised form 20 September 2001; accepted 13 October 2001 Abstract We report paleomagnetic results for Carboniferous rocks from the eastern part of the Hexi Corridor, which we have demonstrated to be the western extension of the North China block (NCB). The characteristic high-temperature remanence component (B-component) exhibits predominantly reverse polarity, and is generally separable by thermal demagnetization temperature steps between 350 and 580‡C. This B-component can also be isolated by alternating fields (AFs) cleaning at a peak value of 20^30 mT using a hybrid thermal^AF demagnetization method. The B-component shows a positive fold test at the 95% confidence level, indicating that it was acquired before Late Triassic to Early Jurassic folding. We interpret the B-component to be of primary origin acquired during the Carboniferous. The corresponding pole positions are at 14.0‡E, 10.5‡N, K95 = 6.2‡ for the Early-Middle Carboniferous (late Visean to Namurian) and at 10.2‡E, 33.3‡N, K95 = 16.7‡ for the Late Carboniferous (Stephanian). Two major folding events occurred, presumably during the Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous and during the Early Ju- rassic to Middle Jurassic, corresponding to the Variscan and Indosinian orogenies, respectively. Indeed, two unconformities can be distinguished in the Alashan/Hexi Corridor terrane, the earlier one between Late Devonian and Early Carbon- iferous sediments, and the later one between Early Jurassic and Middle Jurassic sediments [17]. The Carboniferous system is made up in as- cending order of the Lower Carboniferous Chou- niugou Formation, Middle Carboniferous Jin- gyuan and Yanghugou Formations, and the Upper Carboniferous Taiyuan Formation (Fig. 2). The Lower Carboniferous series unconform- ably overlies the Upper Devonian Zhongning Formation. It is mainly composed of sandy sand- stone and mudstone interbedded with limestone or light-gray and gray limestone. The upper part of this series yields corals (e.g. Yuanophyllum kan- suense, Dibunophyllum bristolens ), brachiopods (Gigantoproductus maxima , Kansuella kansuensis ) and £ora (e.g. Sublepidodendron mirabile , Rhodea hsianghsiangensis), indicating a late Datang age (i.e. late Visean stage, [17]). Two major folding events occurred, presumably during the Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous and during the Early Ju- rassic to Middle Jurassic, corresponding to the Variscan and Indosinian orogenies, respectively. Indeed, two unconformities can be distinguished in the Alashan/Hexi Corridor terrane, the earlier one between Late Devonian and Early Carbon- iferous sediments, and the later one between Early Jurassic and Middle Jurassic sediments [17]. The Carboniferous system is made up in as- cending order of the Lower Carboniferous Chou- niugou Formation, Middle Carboniferous Jin- gyuan and Yanghugou Formations, and the Upper Carboniferous Taiyuan Formation (Fig. 2). The Lower Carboniferous series unconform- ably overlies the Upper Devonian Zhongning Formation. It is mainly composed of sandy sand- stone and mudstone interbedded with limestone or light-gray and gray limestone. The upper part of this series yields corals (e.g. Yuanophyllum kan- suense, Dibunophyllum bristolens ), brachiopods (Gigantoproductus maxima , Kansuella kansuensis ) and £ora (e.g. Sublepidodendron mirabile , Rhodea hsianghsiangensis), indicating a late Datang age (i.e. late Visean stage, [17]). Therefore, the bulk sample experiences far less heating than in convention- al experiments and, consequently, alteration is greatly reduced (e.g. [4]). The microwave/SQUID magnetometer system at Liverpool University, op- erating at a microwave frequency of 8.2 GHz, has been used successfully for palaeointensity studies using ceramics [5,6] and historic lava [4,7]. The NCB was probably independent in terms of dynamics. its drift history was dominant by latitudinal placement ac- companying rotation in the Early Paleozoic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was part of Gondwanaland, and might be close to the YZB and Australia in the Early Paleozoic. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. During Late Permian to Late Triassic, the NCB and YZB were characterized by northern latitudinal placement and ro- tation on the pivot in the Dabie area. The NCB and YZB collided first in the eastern part where they were located at northern latitude of about 6"-8', and a triangular oceanic basin remained in the Late Permian. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic. The NCB was probably independent in terms of dynamics. its drift history was dominant by latitudinal placement ac- companying rotation in the Early Paleozoic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was part of Gondwanaland, and might be close to the YZB and Australia in the Early Paleozoic. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. During Late Permian to Late Triassic, the NCB and YZB were characterized by northern latitudinal placement and ro- tation on the pivot in the Dabie area. The NCB and YZB collided first in the eastern part where they were located at northern latitude of about 6"-8', and a triangular oceanic basin remained in the Late Permian. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic. The NCB was probably independent in terms of dynamics. its drift history was dominant by latitudinal placement ac- companying rotation in the Early Paleozoic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was part of Gondwanaland, and might be close to the YZB and Australia in the Early Paleozoic. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. During Late Permian to Late Triassic, the NCB and YZB were characterized by northern latitudinal placement and ro- tation on the pivot in the Dabie area. The NCB and YZB collided first in the eastern part where they were located at northern latitude of about 6"-8', and a triangular oceanic basin remained in the Late Permian. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. We review and critically assess all the available paleomagnetic data published since the beginning of the 1980s. Paleomagnetic data revealed that the tectonic history of the NCB and YZB was characterized by northern latitudinal displace- ment and rotation pivoted in the east Qinling from the Late Permian to Late Triassic (fig. 4). Fig. 4. Collision and suturation procedure of the NCB and YZB. The westward chap between two blocks was about 70" when they initially collided in the eastern part, while the NCB and Mongolia Block had collided together[lo1. The NCB rotated anticlock- wise due to a continuous push of the Mongolia Block from the Late Permian to Middle Jurassic. The YZB rotated clockwise due to an inertia forcing driven by itself northward drifting in the same period. After that the NCB and YZB were completely sutured and slowly rotated anticlock- wise together. VOI. 41 supp. SCIENCE IN CHINA (Series D) December 1998 Paleomagnetic result of the Lower-Cretaceous from Luanping basin, Hebei Province and its tectonic implications * SUN Zhiming (M\%Pfl), YANG Zhenyu (@jEZ), MA Xinghua (qEq) and ZHAO Yue ( & &!4) (Institute of Geomechanics, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing 100081, China) Received September 16, 1998 Abstract A paleomagnetic study of about 95 samples from 16 sites sampled in the Early Cretaceous in Luanping basin in Hebei Province was reported. Stepwise thermal demagnetization was used to isolate magnetic components. Most samples have a characteristic direction with a high temperature component above 50093 . The tectonic-corrected data are D = 347.8'. I = 50.4'. ass = 7. lo, and the corresponding pole position is at 76. ION, 346.3'E, with dp = 6.4". dm = 3.8', paleolatitude A = 31.1°N. This result indicates a counterclockwise post-Cretaceous rotation of 30.7" + 9.8" with respect to the stable Ordos basin in the west of North China Block, and a non-significant northward mo- tion. This rotation could be related to local fault action or structural detachment, or regional NNW-NWWward motion and collision of Kula-Pacific plate with eastern China since the Early Cret

This rotation could be related to local fault action or structural detachment, or regional NNW-NWWward motion and collision of Kula-Pacific plate with eastern China since the Early Cretaceous. Keywords: Luanping basin, Early Cretaceous, counterclockwise rotation, Kula-Pacific plate. Since the 1980s, a large number of paleomagnetic studies have been carried out in the Ordos basin in the west of North China Block (NCB)['-~]. A number of reliable Jurassic-Cretaceous pa- leomagnetic data have been obtained to establish the apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the whole NCB, and to provide important fundamental information for studying its structural evolu- tion. A lot of geological studies have shown the distinct tectonic differential movement between the eastern and western part of NCB since the Mesozoic. The western part of NCB is character- ized by large Jurassic-Cretaceous fault basin, while the eastern part is characterized by small Mid- dle Jurassic-Cretaceous fault basin, large scale magmatic explosion and intrusion, and severe struc- tural activity. So, paleomagnetic studies may contribute to a better understanding of the Mesozoic evolution of NCB by correlating the Jurassic-Cretaceous paleomagnetic data with that from other tectonic units. A c

nding of the Mesozoic evolution of NCB by correlating the Jurassic-Cretaceous paleomagnetic data with that from other tectonic units. A considerable amount of paleomagnetic studies have been carried out in the Juras- sic-Cretaceous sediments in the eastern part of NCB. It is difficult to interpret the paleomagnetic data because of the complex structure, multi-periodic volcanic activity and widespread remagneti- zation related to the Yanshannian orogeny in this region. In this paper we report the paleomagnet- ic result obtained from lower Cretaceous sediments in Luanping basin, and discuss its tectonic im- plications by comparison with paleomagnetic results from adjacent blocks. 1 Sampling and paleomagnetic measurements The Luanping basin is one of the regions in NCB in which the late Jurassic-early Cretaceous volcanic sediments are well developed. Tectonics Special Research Center, Department of Geology and Geophysics, The University of Western Australia, Perth, WA 6907, Australia Correspondence should be addressed to Zhang Shihong (email: shzhang@cugb.edu.cn) Received August 31, 2000 Abstract A total of 312 oriented core samples collected from the Neoproterozoic to lower Cam- brian strata in the Lushan region of western Henan Province, southern North China Block, were subjected to stepwise demagnetization. After removing recent and possibly Mesozoic overprint components, inferred primary magnetic remanence was isolated from the Precambrian Dongjia, Sanjiaotang and Cuizhuang Formations. Our new results, together with selected previous results, suggest that the North China Block was in low latitudinal positions for most of the studied time in- terval. Through comparison with paleogeographic positions of other continents, we suggest that the NCB could have been closed to Siberia during the ca. 800–600 Ma interval. Keywords: North China Block, Neoproterozoic, paleomagnetism, paleogeography. Palaeomagnetic, rock magnetic and magnetic fabric results are presented for a Carboniferous (Visean to Westphalian) succession of felsic, mainly ignimbritic, volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks from the Rocky Creek Block of the northern Tamworth Belt, southern New England Orogen. Detailed thermal demagnetisation of 734 samples from 64 sites show three groups of magnetic components with low (<300°C), intermediate (300–600°C) and high (500–680°C) unblocking temperature ranges. Well-defined primary magnetisations have been determined for 28 sites with evidence of four overprint phases. The overprints arise from a mid-Tertiary weathering event (or possibly recent viscous origin), and from fluid movements associated with the Late Cretaceous opening of the Tasman Sea, thrusting during the Middle Triassic main phase of the Hunter–Bowen Orogeny, and latest Carboniferous – Early Permian formation of the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system. The overprints arise from a mid-Tertiary weathering event (or possibly recent viscous origin), and from fluid movements associated with the Late Cretaceous opening of the Tasman Sea, thrusting during the Middle Triassic main phase of the Hunter–Bowen Orogeny, and latest Carboniferous – Early Permian formation of the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system. Rock magnetic tests establish that the primary magnetisation carriers in the volcanic rocks are mainly magnetite (predominantly single domain, or pseudo-single domain, and little or no multidomain) and hematite. Optimal magnetic cleaning is achieved at high to very high temperatures, with subtle, but systematic, directional and statistical differences between primary components derived from the mainly hematite fraction and pseudo-components derived from the mainly magnetite fraction. The Peri Rhyolite has been correlated with the Eastons Arm Rhyolite of the southern Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11). The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006 2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag- netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified (Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’). This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. The Peri Rhyolite has been correlated with the Eastons Arm Rhyolite of the southern Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11). The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006 2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag- netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified (Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’). This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite, which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with the Peri Rhyolite. In contrast, Opdyke et al. (2000), follow- ing earlier workers (Hocking 1973; Stroud 1990b), regarded this Boomi Creek succession as a minor thrust sliver belonging to the Caroda Formation. The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000) near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). A SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 310.6/H110064.0 Ma indicates a late Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6). The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite, which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with the Peri Rhyolite. The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000) near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). A SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 310.6/H110064.0 Ma indicates a late Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6). The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. Widespread occurrence of magnetic overprints of Permo-Carboniferous (Schmidt 1988; Klootwijk 1996b) and Permo-Triassic age (Lackie & Schmidt 1993) throughout the Tamworth Belt succession and the Carboniferous succession of the Texas and Coffs Harbour Oroclines (Aubourg et al. 1994) has become well established. Therefore, sampling of the Rocky Creek Block concentrated on the frequent volcanic and tuff-rich volcani- clastic intercalations—ash-flow tuffs, ash-fall tuffs, lavas, tuffites—throughout the upper Lower to Upper Carbon- iferous succession. Sampling of the middle Visean to Westphalian– Stephanian volcanic-rich succession of the Rocky Creek Block (64 sites, 734 samples) has been carried out in three phases. Reconnaissance sampling (17 sites, 171 samples) was carried out in 1987. Preliminary palaeomagnetic results from this collection were listed in Klootwijk (1996a) and their implications were discussed in an initial syn- thesis of the Carboniferous palaeomagnetism of the Tamworth Belt (Klootwijk 1996b). Extensive follow-up sampling (41 sites, 492 samples) was carried out in 1995 for comprehensive stratigraphic coverage of the successions and for fold tests. Sampling was complemented in 1999 with a small collection (6 sites, 71 samples) to strengthen the palaeomagnetic record of the Clifden Formation. This sampling also addressed the stratigraphic position of the Boomi Rhyolite – Kooringal Dacite succession, generally considered part of the Caroda Formation, but interpreted herein as part of the Clifden Formation. The potential of magnetic fabric analysis for determin- ation of transport directions in ignimbrites and trans- ported air-fall tuffs has been well established from pioneering studies on felsic volcanic rocks, mainly Cenozoic, in southwestern North America (MacDonald & Palmer 1990; Palmer et al. 1991). Such studies have shown that the K min axis of the AMS ellipsoid generally represents the pole to the foliation or flow-banding plane, that the K max axis parallels the flow- or transport-axis, and that imbrication of coarser components within the volcanic rocks can be used as an indication of transport direction with the source expected in the downdip direction of imbrication. The method can only be applied reliably if it can be established that the AMS ellipsoids reflect primary depositional patterns and not tectonic deformation. The in situ K max axes of the volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks of the Rocky Creek Block show an overall north– south alignment (Figure 10b). The regional tectonic grain is also north–south (Figures 3, 4) and a tectonic origin of the AMS pattern might, therefore, be surmised at first glance. INTERPRETATION Overprint magnetisations: post-folding MIDDLE–LATE CENOZOIC OVERPRINTS A magnetically soft overprint of exclusively normal polarity and with in situ directions close to the present local field direction is consistently present throughout the sites (Figure 12a, b). This component is unblocked at temperatures up to 300°C and in alternating fields up to 30 mT . Its mean direction is indistinguishable from a present field component in the southward adjacent Werrie Block. Both are similar to an overprint observed on the south coast of New South Wales and interpreted as Early Miocene in age (Nott et al. 1991). This set of over- prints may be indicative of a regional mid-Tertiary weathering event, although the overprints’ exclusive normal polarity and closeness to the present local field direction alternatively may point to a recent viscous origin. SAMPLING Sampling strategy An initial pilot study of the Tamworth Belt succession, on the Lower Carboniferous volcano-sedimentary succession of the Upper Rouchel region, demonstrated that ignimbritic volcanics can retain their primary magnetisation, despite conditions leading to pervasive overprinting of inter- calated volcaniclastic rocks. Widespread occurrence of magnetic overprints of Permo-Carboniferous (Schmidt 1988; Klootwijk 1996b) and Permo-Triassic age (Lackie & Schmidt 1993) throughout the Tamworth Belt succession and the Carboniferous succession of the Texas and Coffs Harbour Oroclines (Aubourg et al. 1994) has become well established. Therefore, sampling of the Rocky Creek Block concentrated on the frequent volcanic and tuff-rich volcani- clastic intercalations—ash-flow tuffs, ash-fall tuffs, lavas, tuffites—throughout the upper Lower to Upper Carbon- iferous succession. Reconnaissance sampling (17 sites, 171 samples) was carried out in 1987. Preliminary palaeomagnetic results from this collection were listed in Klootwijk (1996a) and their implications were discussed in an initial syn- thesis of the Carboniferous palaeomagnetism of the Tamworth Belt (Klootwijk 1996b). Extensive follow-up sampling (41 sites, 492 samples) was carried out in 1995 for comprehensive stratigraphic coverage of the successions and for fold tests. These may have induced magnetic overprints on the studied successions of the Rocky Creek Block, requir- ing careful analysis and interpretation of the palaeo- magnetic data in order to separate and identify primary and overprint components, and perhaps incompletely cleaned pseudo-components. Top and bottom of the specimens were ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen per sample. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: . Well-defined triaxial ellipsoids are also prominent, but various sites do not have a clear magnetic fabric pattern. The potential of magnetic fabric analysis for determin- ation of transport directions in ignimbrites and trans- ported air-fall tuffs has been well established from pioneering studies on felsic volcanic rocks, mainly Cenozoic, in southwestern North America (MacDonald & Palmer 1990; Palmer et al. 1991). Such studies have shown that the K min axis of the AMS ellipsoid generally represents the pole to the foliation or flow-banding plane, that the K max axis parallels the flow- or transport-axis, and that imbrication of coarser components within the volcanic rocks can be used as an indication of transport direction with the source expected in the downdip direction of imbrication. The method can only be applied reliably if it can be established that the AMS ellipsoids reflect primary depositional patterns and not tectonic deformation. The in situ K max axes of the volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks of the Rocky Creek Block show an overall north– south alignment (Figure 10b). The regional tectonic grain is also north–south (Figures 3, 4) and a tectonic origin of the AMS pattern might, therefore, be surmised at first glance. This component is unblocked at temperatures up to 300°C and in alternating fields up to 30 mT . Therefore, sampling of the Rocky Creek Block concentrated on the frequent volcanic and tuff-rich volcani- clastic intercalations—ash-flow tuffs, ash-fall tuffs, lavas, tuffites—throughout the upper Lower to Upper Carbon- iferous succession. Palaeomagnetic, rock magnetic and magnetic fabric results are presented for a Carboniferous (Visean to Westphalian) succession of felsic, mainly ignimbritic, volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks from the Rocky Creek Block of the northern Tamworth Belt, southern New England Orogen. Detailed thermal demagnetisation of 734 samples from 64 sites show three groups of magnetic components with low (<300°C), intermediate (300–600°C) and high (500–680°C) unblocking temperature ranges. Well-defined primary magnetisations have been determined for 28 sites with evidence of four overprint phases. The overprints arise from a mid-Tertiary weathering event (or possibly recent viscous origin), and from fluid movements associated with the Late Cretaceous opening of the Tasman Sea, thrusting during the Middle Triassic main phase of the Hunter–Bowen Orogeny, and latest Carboniferous – Early Permian formation of the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system. The Peri Rhyolite has been correlated with the Eastons Arm Rhyolite of the southern Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11). The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006 2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag- netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified (Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’). This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite, which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with the Peri Rhyolite. In contrast, Opdyke et al. (2000), follow- ing earlier workers (Hocking 1973; Stroud 1990b), regarded this Boomi Creek succession as a minor thrust sliver belonging to the Caroda Formation. The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. Deformation phases The New England Orogen has a long history of tectonic activity . Up to eight tectonic phases have been identified for the period from Devonian to the Late Cretaceous opening of the Tasman Sea (Korsch & Harrington 1981; Harrington & Korsch 1985a; Veevers et al. 1994b; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Tamworth Belt has been affected strongly by four of the phases. These may have induced magnetic overprints on the studied successions of the Rocky Creek Block, requir- ing careful analysis and interpretation of the palaeo- magnetic data in order to separate and identify primary and overprint components, and perhaps incompletely cleaned pseudo-components. The oldest of these four Carboniferous tectonic phases relates to development of the erosional disconformity between the lower and upper succession. Magnetic over- prints close to the top of the eroded succession may result from chemical processes during erosion, or may be due to fluid-flow that used the erosional disconformity as a pathway . The second tectonic phase had a major effect on the shape of the New England Orogen. MAGNETIC TREATMENT, ANALYSIS AND INTERPRETATION METHODS Sample preparation All core samples were sandblasted to remove possible mag- netic contamination from the stainless-steel drill barrels, and were sliced into standard specimens, 2.54 cm diameter and 2.2 cm height. Top and bottom of the specimens were ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen per sample. Alternating-field (AF) demagnetisation was carried out on one representative specimen per site and rock magnetic studies on one other specimen per site. Palaeomagnetic treatment One specimen per sample was subjected to progressive thermal demagnetisation in 18–36 steps up to peak temper- atures of 695°C. Thermal demagnetisation was carried out in large-volume furnaces (McElhinny et al. 1971) at the centre of feedback-controlled Rubens–Helmholtz coil systems (10 coils), which reduce the ambient magnetic field to less than 5 nT over the heating–cooling cycle. The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000) near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). A SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 310.6/H110064.0 Ma indicates a late Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6). The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. Widespread occurrence of magnetic overprints of Permo-Carboniferous (Schmidt 1988; Klootwijk 1996b) and Permo-Triassic age (Lackie & Schmidt 1993) throughout the Tamworth Belt succession and the Carboniferous succession of the Texas and Coffs Harbour Oroclines (Aubourg et al. 1994) has become well established. Therefore, sampling of the Rocky Creek Block concentrated on the frequent volcanic and tuff-rich volcani- clastic intercalations—ash-flow tuffs, ash-fall tuffs, lavas, tuffites—throughout the upper Lower to Upper Carbon- iferous succession. Top and bottom of the specimens were ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen per sample. ate Triassic paleomagnetic studies are required for the Yangtze Block as well as for the NCB. Post-Late Triassic paleomagnetic poles have been computed for areas spread over the Yangtze Block [2,7^9]. The northwestern and southwestern parts of this block were subjected to Cenozoic intra-cratonic deformation [10^12], and paleo- magnetic poles from these areas can not be re- garded as representative of the stable block. It is therefore necessary to establish a characteristic paleomagnetic pole from a tectonically stable part of the Yangtze Block, in order to understand its relationship to the NCB. We have focused in this study on Late Jurassic formations from the Sichuan basin that is consid- ered to be a stable part of the Yangtze Block. Brief reviews and some geodynamic interpretation of the development of this region are given by Zubkov et al. (1989) and Ashchepkov et al. (1995). A ring of Mesozoic - Cenozoic alkaline-basalt volcanism has been found at the northern margin Minusinsk Depression. The volcanic pipes and dikes arc grouped over the margins of Kopievo dome-shaped uplift and located near flexures and main faults (Fig.1). These volcanic bodies represent the root system of volcanic eruptions, forming volcanic pipes of complex structure, lava necks and numerous dikes. Pipes mostly are multiphase structures composed of eruptive breccias with altered groundmass containing abundant debris of basalts and hypabyssal basanites. No cover facies have been identified. Despite textural variety of the basalts, their chemical composition remains constant, and they are all classed as basanites. The volcanic rocks have been intruded into Devonian- Carboniferous age terrigenous deposits. The K-Ar isotopic ages (Zubkov et al., 1989) for these four volcanic pipes are found within the range of 71-45 Ma. Two volcanoes (Bele and Tergeshskaya pipes), 545 546 V.Yu. Davidson a aSchool of Geology and Geophysics, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK 73119, USA bDepartment of Geology and Petroleum Geology, University of Aberdeen, King’s College, Aberdeen AB24 3UE Scotland, UK Abstract Paleomagnetic results suggest that there was a ﬂuid-ﬂow event which caused dolomitization and hematite authigenesis in serpentinite within the Highland Border Group along the Highland Boundary Fault in central Scotland in the late Carboniferous/ early Permian. Geochemical data indicate that the ﬂuid was hydrothermal in origin, and in addition to causing hematite authigenesis, the ﬂuid also thermally remagnetized pre-existing magnetite in the serpentinite. q 2000 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved. Keywords: remagnetization; ﬂuids; fault; paleomagnetism 1. Introduction In central Scotland, there are numerous exposures of red dolomite in the Caledonian (pre

HBF) in the Lower Paleozoic Highland Border Group (HBG). This study uses paleomagnetic analysis to date the ﬂuid migration event responsible for the dolomitiza- tion in the HBG and to assess whether the dolomite represents a single episode of ﬂuid-ﬂow and alteration of the basement, or if there were multiple events that are juxtaposed coincidentally. 2. Geological setting The trace of the HBF can be mapped with conﬁ- dence for a distance of 230 km from Stonehaven to Arran in central Scotland (Fig. 1). The predominant rocks to the north of the fault are Dalradian metasedi- ments whereas the rocks to the south are continental Devonian (Old Red Sandstone, ORS) sediments. At many places there is a narrow outcrop of the HBG, immediately south of the fault plane. These rocks represent an oceanic or backarc assemblage that has been excised almost completely. It includes several exposures of serpentinite, representing sea-ﬂoor basic rocks altered by meteoric ﬂuids (Ikin and Harmon, 1983). In some outcrops the serpentinite is massive. In others it is brecciated, either due to tectonic activity or synsedimentary processes. Outcrops of the serpentinite exhibit extensive dolo- mitization and/or siliciﬁcation. The alteration occurs partly as a massive replacement and partly as thin (from 1 to ,10 cm)

. Petrographic and geochemical studies are underway to assess this possibility. In summary, the results from the fault zone rocks in the HBF indicate that there was at least one dolomi- tizing and hematite-precipitating ﬂuid alteration event in central Scotland in the late Carboniferous. Measurement of the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility on the gabbroic samples reveals a flat-lying foliation with a radiating pattern of lineations, supporting the field evidence that the gabbros are part of a large, undeformed sill. Petrographic observations of oxides in the gabbros reveals two populations of magnetite grains produced during the original cooling of the sill: large, oxyexsolved titanomagnetite grains and fine-grained magnetite in igneous reaction rims. New 40Ar/39Ar age dating of biotite and plagioclase yield ages of V1.2 Ga, which represent the rapid cooling following emplacement of the mafic magma. PALEOMAGNETIC ANALYSIS Procedure and technique. In the second half of the 1980s, we gathered collections from Lakhandinskaya Group exposures which were treated, at that time, in the following way. A pilot collection (usually 25%–30% of the total number of samples) was randomly selected for each exposure. The pilot collection was subjected to detailed thermal demagnetization, and its results were used to choose an optimum regime of demagnetization, i.e., the temperature at which, supposedly, only the characteristic component remained in the sample. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. The following rejection criteria were employed: small signal values comparable with the instrumentation noise,

an 3–6 nT were used for the sample demagnetization. The remanent magnetization was measured on cryogenic magnetometers manufactured by 2G Enterprises and CTF. The paleomagnetic poles from the study rocks clearly differ from younger poles of the Siberian Platform. All these data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component was acquired at the time of or shortly after the deposition of the Lakhandinskaya Group. Taking into account recent paleomagnetic data on the Middle Riphean Malginskaya Formation, results of this current work suggest, depending on the choice of the paleomagnetic direction polarity, two possible scenarios for relative movements of the Siberian Platform and Laurentia in a 1100–1000-Ma interval. One of these scenarios contradicts the hypothesis on Siberia as a part of the Rodinia supercontinent. A pilot collection (usually 25%–30% of the total number of samples) was randomly selected for each exposure. The pilot collection was subjected to detailed thermal demagnetization, and its results were used to choose an optimum regime of demagnetization, i.e., the temperature at which, supposedly, only the characteristic component remained in the sample. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. Nevertheless, unlike the recon- structions proposed by these authors, our data required that Siberia be rotated so as to juxtapose its south- southeastern part and the northern and northeastern parts of Laurentia. In order to verify the validity of the model proposed, it was necessary to compare the paleomagnetic poles of Siberia and Laurentia for other time levels. In order to verify the validity of the model proposed, it was necessary to compare the paleomagnetic poles of Siberia and Laurentia for other time levels. A pilot collection (usually 25%–30% of the total number of samples) was randomly selected for each exposure. The pilot collection was subjected to detailed thermal demagnetization, and its results were used to choose an optimum regime of demagnetization, i.e., the temperature at which, supposedly, only the characteristic component remained in the sample. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. The following rejection criteria were employed: small signal values comparable with the instrumentation noise,

an 3–6 nT were used for the sample demagnetization. The remanent magnetization was measured on cryogenic magnetometers manufactured by 2G Enterprises and CTF. DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. The paleomagnetic poles from the study rocks clearly differ from younger poles of the Siberian Platform. All these data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component was acquired at the time of or shortly after the deposition of the Lakhandinskaya Group. Taking into account recent paleomagnetic data on the Middle Riphean Malginskaya Formation, results of this current work suggest, depending on the choice of the paleomagnetic direction polarity, two possible scenarios for relative movements of the Siberian Platform and Laurentia in a 1100–1000-Ma interval. One of these scenarios contradicts the hypothesis on Siberia as a part of the Rodinia supercontinent. The second scenario, which implies a variation in the generally accepted polarity for one of the cratonic blocks considered, is in a good agreement with this hypothesis but requires a coincidence of northern Laurentia with south-southeastern Siberia, rather than with its northern part, as is assumed in most reconstructions. DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. The paleomagnetic poles from the study rocks clearly differ from younger poles of the Siberian Platform. All these data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component was acquired at the time of or shortly after the deposition of the Lakhandinskaya Group. Taking into account recent paleomagnetic data on the Middle Riphean Malginskaya Formation, results of this current work suggest, depending on the choice of the paleomagnetic direction polarity, two possible scenarios for relative movements of the Siberian Platform and Laurentia in a 1100–1000-Ma interval. One of these scenarios contradicts the hypothesis on Siberia as a part of the Rodinia supercontinent. The second scenario, which implies a variation in the generally accepted polarity for one of the cratonic blocks considered, is in a good agreement with this hypothesis but requires a coincidence of northern Laurentia with south-southeastern Siberia, rather than with its northern part, as is assumed in most reconstructions. Brecciation The M-JC ore-bearing structures consist of two interrelated types of breccia bodies. ‘‘Breakthrough’’ structures cut one or more stratigraphic units. They are discordant bodies up to several thousand meters long, up to a few hundred meters wide, and up to >150 m high (Hoagland et al., 1965; Crawford et al., 1969). They may be V-shaped, low-domal or high- domal structures that appear to follow pre-mineralisa- tion faults and joints, and that are filled with a rubble breccia containing several petrographic types of clasts (McCormick et al., 1971; Hill, 1969; Hill et al., 1971a; Hoagland, 1976). Crackle breccias are found around the top and sides of the breakthrough struc- tures. The Immel, Young and New Market ore bodies are in ‘‘breakthrough’’ breccias. ‘‘Bedded’’ structures occur only within certain limestone beds in the King- sport Formation. They are semi-concordant tabular mantos of dolomitisation, brecciation and mineralisa- tion that appear to extend laterally from breakthrough breccia bodies in most cases (Kendall, 1960; Ful- weiler and McDougal, 1971). These bedded bodies rarely exceed more than tens of meters wide in length Fig. 3.

Brecciation The M-JC ore-bearing structures consist of two interrelated types of breccia bodies. ‘‘Breakthrough’’ structures cut one or more stratigraphic units. They are discordant bodies up to several thousand meters long, up to a few hundred meters wide, and up to >150 m high (Hoagland et al., 1965; Crawford et al., 1969). They may be V-shaped, low-domal or high- domal structures that appear to follow pre-mineralisa- tion faults and joints, and that are filled with a rubble breccia containing several petrographic types of clasts (McCormick et al., 1971; Hill, 1969; Hill et al., 1971a; Hoagland, 1976). Crackle breccias are found around the top and sides of the breakthrough struc- tures. The Immel, Young and New Market ore bodies are in ‘‘breakthrough’’ breccias. ‘‘Bedded’’ structures occur only within certain limestone beds in the King- sport Formation. They are semi-concordant tabular mantos of dolomitisation, brecciation and mineralisa- tion that appear to extend laterally from breakthrough breccia bodies in most cases (Kendall, 1960; Ful- weiler and McDougal, 1971). These bedded bodies rarely exceed more than tens of meters wide in length Fig. 3.

Brecciation The M-JC ore-bearing structures consist of two interrelated types of breccia bodies. ‘‘Breakthrough’’ structures cut one or more stratigraphic units. They are discordant bodies up to several thousand meters long, up to a few hundred meters wide, and up to >150 m high (Hoagland et al., 1965; Crawford et al., 1969). They may be V-shaped, low-domal or high- domal structures that appear to follow pre-mineralisa- tion faults and joints, and that are filled with a rubble breccia containing several petrographic types of clasts (McCormick et al., 1971; Hill, 1969; Hill et al., 1971a; Hoagland, 1976). Crackle breccias are found around the top and sides of the breakthrough struc- tures. The Immel, Young and New Market ore bodies are in ‘‘breakthrough’’ breccias. ‘‘Bedded’’ structures occur only within certain limestone beds in the King- sport Formation. They are semi-concordant tabular mantos of dolomitisation, brecciation and mineralisa- tion that appear to extend laterally from breakthrough breccia bodies in most cases (Kendall, 1960; Ful- weiler and McDougal, 1971). These bedded bodies rarely exceed more than tens of meters wide in length Fig. 3.

art of the Kisseynew Domain of the Trans-Hudson Orogen (THO) in north-central Manitoba. The dome is circular, about 6 km in diameter, with steeply-dipping flanks. It is composed of upper amphibolite-facies gneisses derived from turbiditic sediments, with leucogranitic sill-like intru - sions that were metamorphosed, starting at about 1830 Ma. Alternating field and thermal step demagnetization of 153 specimens from 17 sites around the perimeter of the dome isolated a characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) di - rection of D = 346.6°, I = 78.9° ( a 95 = 5.3°, k = 46, N = 17) that gives a pole of 119.5° W, 75.8° N ( dp = 9.5°, dm = 10.0°). Unblocking temperatures and saturation isothermal remanence analyses show that the ChRM resides mostly in single to pseudosingle domain magnetite or titanomagnetite, with minor hematite commonly present and with minor pyrrhotite present in the leucogranites. This Wapisu gneiss dome paleopole is the first from the Kisseynew Domain and the first from the 1830 to 1770 Ma interval in the THO. It indicates an ~90° bend or hair - pin in the apparent polar wander path for the THO juvenile terranes and Superior craton. It is speculated

At 72% unfolding, the Williston paleopole is rotated by 10 ± 12° clockwise with respect to the Early Cretaceous North America reference paleopole (124–88 Ma) of Van Fossen and Kent (1992; latitude 71.2°N, longitude 194.1°E), whereas at 100% unfolding the Williston paleopole is rotated by 19 ± 10° counterclockwise from this reference pole. At 87% unfolding, where directional grouping is best, the angular distance between the Williston and Cretaceous reference paleopoles is 7.5 ± 9°, whereas at 80% unfolding the paleopoles are also statistically indistin - guishable (Fig. 8). We suggest that Triassic rocks at Williston Lake were remagnetized during the initial stages of the Cretaceous– Cenozoic Laramide orogenic phase between 72 and 100% unfolding. The exclusive occurrence of normal polarity directions can then be reconciled with remanence acquisition during either the Cretaceous long normal superchron, a period of the Earth’s magnetic field from about 118 to 84 Ma characterized by stable normal polarity, or perhaps one of the somewhat shorter, but still appreciable in length, normal polarity chrons in the Late Cretaceous (e.g., C33n). In Late Cretaceous times, greater India broke away from Madagascar with voluminous igneous activity accompanying the continental break-up. A geochemi- cal study of the Madagascan flood basalts suggests that the Marion hot spot was an important source of melts at the southern end of the island (Mahoney et a/., 1991; Storey et a/., 1997). This is also supported by a palaeogeographic reconstruction placing Mada- gascar in the near vicinity of the Marion hot spot around Late Cretaceous times (Storey et a/., 1995; Torsvik et a/., 1998). GEOLOGY OF NICARAGUA Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben (McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1

, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivision of the Coyol Group. To the west of the depression, in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain, the rocks are predominantly of sedimentary origin and are assumed to have been deposited on a Nicoya Complex type of basement (Parsons Corporation Report 1972). The sediments, tuffaceous shale, siltstone, greywacke, sandstone and lime- stone, range in age from Cretaceous to Miocene (Rivas, Brito, Masachapa and El Fraile formations) and are overlain by sediments of similar composition to the El Salto Formation and the pyroclastic deposits of the La Sierra Group (McBirney & Williams 1965; Parsons Corporation Report 1972). Seyfried et al. (1987) regard the Upper Cretaceous Rivas and the Eocene Brito formations as parts of a continuous succession. The Masachapa Formation is Oligocene in age (Auer 1942, unpublished paper; Zoppis Bracci & Del Guidice 1958) and the boundary between the Brito and Masachapa formations has been interpreted as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965). Also, the contact between the Masachapa Formation and the overlying Miocene El Fraile Formation is regarded as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965; Kuang 1971) and the El Fraile Formation interﬁngers with part of the volcanic Tamarindo Formation. As the tectonic control was often poor, our ambition has been to collect samples of rocks of similar age but geographically well-separated in order to detect later local tectonic movements. To the west of the Nicaraguan Depression we collected sedimentary and intrusive rocks of the Rivas Formation, sedi- mentary rocks of the Brito Formation and volcanic rocks of the Tamarindo Formation. The ages of these formations are Upper Cretaceous, Eocene and Miocene–Pliocene, respectively. MINERALOGICAL STUDIES Petrographic and X-ray diffraction studies (Nystro ¨m & Levi 1985; Elming 1985) have been carried out on specimens of andesite, basalt and sedimentary rocks from a number of sites. Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite, is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Alth

section_candidates.excerpt: RAGUA Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben (McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation Report 1972), characterized by basaltic rocks overlain by inter- mediate to acid volcanic rocks. Ehrenborg (1996) has explained the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivis

As weathering is a particular problem in tropical areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite, is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation Report 1972), characterized by basaltic r

s formations . These breaks were suggested to reﬂect tectonic events of regional character (Levi et al. 1990), possibly related to changes in the polarity of subduction. PALAEOMAGNETIC SAMPLING Samples for the present study were collected from the Nicaraguan Highland and from the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain. The study includes some 245 samples from 30 sites (Fig. 3), collected as block samples or with a portable drill, and oriented with sun or magnetic compasses. Generally, each sampling site represents a 10–20 m 2-scale outcrop. The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. Age summary Based on our new geochronological evidence, most of the samples dated by the 40Ar /39Ar method show either signiﬁcant argon loss or signiﬁcant argon gain. If these signs of alteration are prevalent throughout the sample suite, then interpretation of the K–Ar ages is difﬁcult. To the west of the Nicaraguan Depression we collected sedimentary and intrusive rocks of the Rivas Formation, sedi- mentary rocks of the Brito Formation and volcanic rocks of the Tamarindo Formation. The ages of these formations are Upper Cretaceous, Eocene and Miocene–Pliocene, respectively. MINERALOGICAL STUDIES Petrographic and X-ray diffraction studies (Nystro ¨m & Levi 1985; Elming 1985) have been carried out on specimens of andesite, basalt and sedimentary rocks from a number of sites. Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite, is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Although the remanent magnetization of haematite is usually more resistant to demagnetization than magnetite, no signiﬁcant relation between degree of martitization and directional variations of the characteristic magnetizations was found. The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation Report 1972), characterized by basaltic rocks overlain by inter- mediate to acid volcanic rocks. Ehrenborg (1996) has explained the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivision of the Coyol Group. The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation Report 1972), characterized by basaltic rocks overlain by inter- mediate to acid volcanic rocks. The secondary minerals show a vertical zoning typical of burial diagenesis, which is a process controlled by an increase in temperature with depth. A palaeo- thermal gradient of about 15–20 uCk m x1 is estimated for the Cretaceous to Oligocene diagenetic episodes and the temper- ature in the lower parts of the Rivas, Brito and Masachapa formations is estimated at c. 120 uC. Levels of various ages, ranging from the Silurian to the Albian, were analysed. These studies led to the determination of ﬁve new African palaeomagnetic poles. The ﬁrst, determined in the ‘El Adeb Larache’ area, is of Moscovian age (Henryet al. 1992), the second is of Stephano–Autunian age from the Tiguentourine For

, the third is from the Middle Zarzaı¨tine Formation of Liassic–Dogger age (Derder et al . 1994b), the fourth, determined in the ‘la Recule´e’ area from the Lower Zarzaitine is of Triassic–Liassic age (Kieset al. 1995), and the ﬁfth is of Bashkirian age from the Oubarakat Formation (Derder et al. 2001a). These studies also showed the existence of Cenozoic and Permian remagnetization events. However, as in most of the palaeomagnetic studies in hori- zontal tabular areas, the age of the magnetization acquisition has not been demonstrated. Indeed, in all cases, geological and geophysical constraints did not permit palaeomagnetic tests, except a reversal test in the Lower Zarzaı ¨tine Formation of Triassic–Liassic age (Kies et al. 1995). Such a reversal test is not absolute proof of the primary character of the magnetization, but indicates that the magnetization consists of a single com- ponent. The only argument in favour of the primary character of the magnetization is the variation of its direction from one formation to another, while the magnetic overprints (Permian and Cenozoic) observed at some levels have the same orientation in the different geological formations. INTRODUCTION The southwestern margin of Gondwanaland was located north of the Colorado River during the Palaeozoic, and marks the boundary between the South America craton to the north and the Patagonia region to the south (Fig. 1). The Sierras Australes orogenic belt trends approximately NW–SE in the southwestern part of Buenos Aires province (Figs 1 and 2), and is considered to be the South American counterpart of the Cape Fold Belt in South Africa (Du Toit 1927). Its geological features have attracted the attention of many geologists since the early 1900s because it is a key to understanding the controversial evolution of this part of Gondwana. For some authors, the Sierras Australes are the result of intracontinental deformation exclusively (Selle´s Martı´nez 1989; Cobbold et al. 1991; Japas 1989); for others, the Sierras Australes are the result of the collision of the Patagonia terrane with Gondwana (Dalmayrac et al . 1980; Ramos 1984; Tomezzoli 1997). The deforma

alaeomagnetic study was to obtain additional reliable palaeomagnetic poles to evaluate the palaeogeographic and geo- dynamic evolution of this area, and therefore of Gondwana, building on the earlier study of Tomezzoli & Vilas (1999). Some investigators have suggested that there may have been more than one tectonic phase in this area, and postulated an early deformation phase of Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous age that preceded the widely recognized Upper Palaeozoic phase (Kilmurray 1975; Varela 1978; Ramos 1984, 1988; Tomezzoli 1997). Tomezzoli & Vilas (1999) reported the presence of a syn- tectonic magnetization carried by haematite (at 42 per cent unfolding) in the red sandstone and clay siltstone of the lower part of the Tunas Formation in the Sierra de las Tunas region (Fig. 2). They concluded that the lower part of the Tunas Formation was deformed and remagnetized very soon after its deposition in the Early Permian. According to Ramos (1984), along the northern boundary of Patagonia and southern margin of Gondwana, an ocean was consumed by subduction beneath Patagonia, the subduction ceasing with the collision of the continental blocks. As a consequence of this collision, deformation in the Sierras Australes may have started in the mid-Palaeozoic. Available palaeoma

na associations of the Tunas Formation indicate an Early Permian to early Late Permian age for these rocks (Harrington 1947; Archangelsky & Cu´ neo 1984). This formation comprises over 1200 m of siliciﬁed ﬁne pale green sandstone and lithic feldsarenite interbedded with red clay–siltstone and shale, which were part of a deltaic complex prograding towards the northeast (Harrington 1947; Andreis et al. 1979; Andreis & Cladera 1992; Lo´ pez Gamundi et al. 1995). Fossil leaves and tuffaceous intervals are present. A characteristic of the shale and ﬁne sandstone is the presence of red sediments, which according to Andreis et al . (1979) con- tain haematite as identiﬁed both by X-ray diffractometry and optically. The Tunas Formation is differentiated from other formations on the basis of its different compositional suite, a well-deﬁned northeastward palaeocurrent pattern, and different depositional conditions. The palaeocurrent data suggest a uni- modal distribution with ﬂow from the southwest towards the northeast (Lo´ pez Gamundi et al. 1995). The strata are older in the western areas (e.g. the San Carlos palaeomagnetic sampling locality shown in Fig. 2) and younger towards the east (e.g. Las Mostazas palaeomagnetic locality in Fig. 2). Some investigators have suggested that there may have been more than one tectonic phase in this area, and postulated an early deformation phase of Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous age that preceded the widely recognized Upper Palaeozoic phase (Kilmurray 1975; Varela 1978; Ramos 1984, 1988; Tomezzoli 1997). Tomezzoli & Vilas (1999) reported the presence of a syn- tectonic magnetization carried by haematite (at 42 per cent unfolding) in the red sandstone and clay siltstone of the lower part of the Tunas Formation in the Sierra de las Tunas region (Fig. 2). They concluded that the lower part of the Tunas Formation was deformed and remagnetized very soon after its deposition in the Early Permian. According to Ramos (1984), along the northern boundary of Patagonia and southern margin of Gondwana, an ocean was consumed by subduction beneath Patagonia, the subduction ceasing with the collision of the continental blocks. In some samples from Las Mostazas, the demagnetization paths were curved, along great circles towards the southeast quadrant with positive inclination, indicating simultaneous removal of distinct mag- netic components with overlapping unblocking temperatures (Fig. 3d). Assuming this, the method of McFadden & McElhinny (1988) was used to analyse these cases. Unblocking temper- atures of samples from the Las Mostazas locality range between 450 and 680 uC, showing that this magnetization is carried by magnetite, haematite or both. Further rock-magnetic studies are required to conﬁrm the magneto-mineralogy. The difference between the magnetic behaviour of samples from this locality and the others is thought to be related to the different carriers of the magnetization, perhaps environmentally controlled in the depositional basin, recalling that the Las Mostazas locality corresponds to the upper level of the sampled units. Demagnetization at high temperatures isolated a reversed characteristic remanent magnetization, consistent with magnetization acquired during the Kiaman reverse superchron.
